title: Depreciation
examples: What is the difference between straight-line and reducing balance?
If I sell equipment, how do I account for the loss?
Do I calculate depreciation on the purchase price or the book value?

explain.say: Today we will learn about depreciation in accounting.
The straight-line method spreads the cost evenly each year.
For example, if a machine costs one thousand pounds and lasts five years, you charge two hundred pounds each year.
The reducing balance method charges more in early years.
A real-life example is a car losing value over time.
When disposing of an asset, you compare its book value to the sale price.

draw.text: Disposal: Book Value vs Sale Price

faq.q: What is the book value of an asset?
faq.a: The book value is the asset's original cost minus the total accumulated depreciation charged so far. You might also ask: What is the carrying amount? Or, what is the net book value?
asks: How do I find the book value?
What is the asset's value on paper?

faq.q: Which method, straight-line or reducing balance, is better?
faq.a: Neither method is inherently better; it depends on how the asset actually loses value. Some assets lose value faster when new, making reducing balance suitable. You could also ask: Which method is more accurate?
asks: Is there a right way to depreciate?
When should I use one method over another?

faq.q: Do I have to use the same method every year?
faq.a: Yes, for consistency in accounting records, you should generally stick to one method once you start. You might ask: Can I change methods later? Or, is consistency required?
asks: Must I keep using the same method?
What if I want to switch methods?

faq.q: What if the asset is fully written off?
faq.a: If the asset's book value reaches zero, you stop charging depreciation on it. You might ask: What happens when it hits zero? Or, can it be fully written off?
asks: Can the book value be negative?

faq.q: How do I calculate the loss on disposal?
faq.a: You compare the asset's book value on the day of sale to the actual cash received. If the sale price is less, it is a loss. You might also ask: What is the profit or loss calculation?
asks: How do I record selling an old machine?
Do I calculate profit or loss on disposal?

facts: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life.
The straight-line method charges equal depreciation amounts every year.
The reducing balance method charges a higher amount in the early years.
When disposing of an asset, the difference between book value and sale price is a profit or loss.

quiz.say: A computer costs £4,000 and is expected to last for 5 years. Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation charge?
quiz.why: The straight-line method divides the total cost by the useful life to get an equal annual charge.

wrong.0: This multiplies the cost by the life, which is too high.
wrong.2: This is the original cost, not the annual charge.
wrong.3: Subtracting the cost from the depreciation is incorrect.

quiz.say: A piece of machinery has a book value of £1,200. If it is sold for £1,000, what is the resulting loss?
quiz.why: A loss occurs when the book value is greater than the cash received from the sale.

wrong.0: Subtracting an extra amount is not part of the calculation.
wrong.1: This gives a negative number, but the loss is measured positively.
wrong.3: Adding the values does not calculate the difference.

quiz.say: If the reducing balance method is used, what happens to the depreciation charge in later years compared to the first year?

options.show: The charge is zero after five years
options.say: The charge is zero after five years

quiz.why: The reducing balance method calculates depreciation on the remaining book value, which gets smaller each year.

wrong.1: This describes the straight-line method, not reducing balance.
wrong.2: This is incorrect; the charge generally falls as the asset ages.
wrong.3: While it approaches zero, it is not necessarily zero until disposal.
